person_made_it: Two scripts that disagree with each other about how to present the same 29 images, one opening on a single frame and the other opening by handing the room its own objections; a template produces one presentation outline, not an argument that there are two right answers.
emcee_who_is_speaking: A hard timecode rail down the left in red monospace, so at any point on the page you know who is talking and how long they have; the spoken words are the only thing set large, and cues are in a different color and voice so nobody reads a stage direction out loud.
what_time_of_day_is_this_room: Monday 5 October, 10am, twelve people and a visible timer. Paper white, because this gets printed and held.
did_the_click_pay_me: Yes: the runtime banner on each version tells you before you read a word whether this shape fits your slot, which is the first question a team actually has.
works_for_the_recipient: It holds at 390px by collapsing the rail above each block, needs no JavaScript, and every term a speaker says out loud is underlined so a nervous presenter can find them while scanning.
taught_me_something: That a presentation script is a timing document, and that writing one without counting the words produces exactly the defect this page was built to fix: my first draft claimed a 5:00 rail over 3.2 minutes of speech.
told_me_the_truth: Yes: the timecodes are computed from real word counts at a stated rate plus a stated pause budget, the footer says so, and the speaker names are flagged as invented placeholders rather than implying real students.
weakest: Both scripts are about the one board with the most material on it, The Last Sitting, so a team whose board is thinner sees two performances that had an easier job than theirs; a third short version built on a deliberately weaker board would prove more.
